answer.body:
One supported criticism concerns J’s sentence:

> “The objection targets the stronger claim that the interval is exact, convex, or decision-sufficient.”

The antecedent is “P9’s compatibility objection.” But P9 itself separates the compatibility/correlation point from the downstream-policy criticism. It says:

> “That gives an interval, but intervals lose correlations: booking A’s high alternative might be incompatible with booking B’s high alternative if they share a physical resource not named in the snapshot. The snapshot does not name physical resources, so this incompatibility is invisible.”

and then, as a distinct criticism:

> “A criticism: exposing alternatives without a policy for resolving them pushes the problem downstream, where it may be resolved badly or inconsistently.”

The first criticism is conditional on a hidden cross-booking resource constraint. The second is not. Even with no hidden resource incompatibility at all, exposing unresolved alternatives without a resolution policy can still push the problem downstream. Conversely, a hidden incompatibility can make an interval loose or non-convex without making it decision-insufficient relative to some downstream threshold.

A distinguishing case: suppose there is no cross-booking incompatibility, but a downstream consumer needs one availability number. The compatibility objection has no purchase, yet P9’s downstream-policy criticism still applies. Conversely, suppose two bookings have alternatives that are jointly incompatible, but the downstream decision only asks whether availability is positive. The compatibility objection refutes an exact/envelope reading of the interval, but the interval may still be decision-sufficient. So “decision-sufficient” is not simply a stronger version of the same bound/envelope claim targeted by the compatibility objection. It is an independent property relative to a decision context.

J later partly acknowledges this when it says:

> “Decision commitment and resource model included: the objection expands into a downstream-policy criticism.”

That charitable reading can be made consistent with P9. But the earlier sentence, “the objection targets … decision-sufficient,” collapses the compatibility objection and the downstream-policy objection into one scale of “claim force.” That loses a distinction the operator question explicitly asks to preserve: “exposing alternatives and objecting to downstream resolution are disputed positions.” The defect is established for the literal reading of J’s sentence; under the more charitable reading, J is making an unmarked addition rather than accurately reporting what the compatibility objection targets.

A second, more local defect also appears in J’s RSS grounding. J says:

> “in RSS terms, an account can be represented as a viewpoint, a reading, a projection, and a set of accepted conjectures.”

But RSS says:

> “An account is a viewpoint, a reading, and a set of accepted conjectures.”

and defines projection separately:

> “Projection: a function from a viewpoint and a reading to a single answer (for example, a single availability number). Projections are allowed but not privileged.”

So J adds projection to the account and then says:

> “RSS’s projection primitive lets us ask what claim about that object is being criticized.”

RSS’s projection primitive does not carry the bound/envelope/decision distinction. It maps a viewpoint and reading to a single answer. An interval [L,U] is not a single answer, and the difference between a bound claim, an envelope claim, and a decision claim is a difference in what is conjectured or committed about the interval, not a difference in the projection function. That work belongs to RSS’s conjecture/commitment vocabulary, not its projection primitive. If J means to extend RSS so that projections can output intervals or so that accounts include projections, that extension should be marked as an addition rather than attributed to RSS “in RSS terms.”
